newsitem.title: UK: UK output, price data do not alter policy dilemma.
newsitem.headline: UK output, price data do not alter policy dilemma.

text.p: British manufacturing output and producer price data for April and May show output is holding up despite the strong pound and inflationary pressures are subdued, but they do not alter the policy dilemma confronting the authorities, economists said.

While the figures are broadly encouraging, they will do little to change the Bank of England's assessment that economic growth is running above trend and will lead to a resurgence in inflation in the medium term if it is not checked.

The problem remains whether rampant consumer demand should be dampened primarily by higher interest rates, which could push sterling even higher and hurt exporters more than it has done to date, or through a fiscal tightening.
"The rebound in manufacturing was encouraging," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International.

"It is presumably being dragged up by domestic demand and sterling is not much of a constraint on exports. It is still lagging domestic demand, but there are some signs of life in domestic production."
Manufacturing output was up 0.6 percent in April from the previous month and 2.3 percent higher year-on-year, while overall industrial production was up 1.2 percent and 2.2 percent respectively.

Shepperd said May producer price numbers were as expected, with core output prices up 0.5 percent year-on-year for the fourth month in a row. "There sems to be very little inflation pressure at the factory gate level," he said.
Dharshini David of HSBC Markets said the output figures confirmed that the recovery in manufacturing remained on track.

"Nevertheless, it would be premature to assume that manufacturing has escaped the effects of sterling's rise relatively lightly, as the worst is almost certainly yet to come," she said. "Accordingly, the policy dilemma that has confronted the authorities over the last few months remains."
Shepperd said the two sets of data had little implications either for next month's monetary meeting or for Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget on July 2.
He sees the possibility of one further increase in interest rates after Friday's quarter-point increase to 6.5 percent.

"The conventional wisdom is that the best way to square the circle of strong domestic demand, but weak output, and strong sterling and pressure on interest rates, is some degree of fiscal restraint," Shepperd said.
"This would take some of the heat out of the retail sector. and perhaps allow sterling to slip back."

Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc, also expects one more rate rise this year. "My central view is 6.75 percent by year-end, but that does embody an assumption that we will have some fiscal tightening in the budget directed at the consumer," he told Reuters Financial Television.
"It also assumes that we are going to get some slowdown in the economyfrom the strength of sterling. But there are some upward risks to that forecast, quite plainly."
David Coleman of CIBC Wood Gundy said there was little in the PPI numbers to change the perception of a competitive pricing environment at the factory gate level.
Headline output prices were running at a level consistent with an annualised rate of less than 1.5 percent while robust gains in input costs largely reflected increases in selected commodity prices.
"If there is a worry, it is that a recovery in manufacturing output, riven by stronger domestic demand, could eventually feed through to firms' price lists," Coleman said.
"But there is no sign of this yet and no indication that the Bank of England, under the new policy regime, would be willing to allow such a development to persist for very long."

Simon Briscoe of Nikko Europe Plc said the rise in total output price inflation to an unadjusted one percent per year in May was due to a small rise in oil prices and was not a worry as it should prove temporary. "The input inflation outlook also remains highly encouraging," he said.
Briscoe said it was not yet clear which variables the Bank of England's new monetary policy committee would pay particular attention to in forming a view on interest rates.
"We feel that these figures ought to be given weight," he said. "They are the best lead indicators of inflation and they show that there is no inflationary pressure."
